notes: Extradition appeal on section 64 trans-frontier conduct; appeal dismissed with leave refused.

enrichment.short_title: Convery: extradition appeal on trans-frontier drug export offences to the Netherlands
key_facts: Mark Convery was sought by Dutch authorities under a European arrest warrant for alleged export of MDMA, amphetamine and cannabis from the Netherlands to the UK.
He had been arrested in the UK on unrelated drug charges that were later discontinued before the Dutch warrant led to extradition proceedings.
A Bow Street district judge ordered extradition on 6 December 2004 after finding the offences were extradition offences and procedural requirements satisfied.
Convery appealed under section 26, arguing time-limit breaches and that conduct partly occurring in the UK could not be an extradition offence under section 64.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 26 of the Extradition Act 2003 against a district judge's extradition order in Category 1 proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; leave to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where a warrant particularises export conduct in a Category 1 territory with possible UK elements, the offences may constitute extradition offences under section 64(3) even if section 64(2) is not satisfied; procedural time limits under section 8 and the practice direction were complied with or could properly be extended.
legal_issues: Whether extradition hearing and appeal time limits under the 2003 Act and practice direction were breached
Whether conduct alleged partly in the United Kingdom could be an extradition offence under section 64
The distinction between sections 64(2) and 64(3) for trans-frontier offences
Whether Cando Armas should be followed on the construction of section 64

confidence.notes: Statutory construction, chronology and final disposition are clearly reasoned by the Divisional Court.

notes: Kava-kava ban challenge; Court of Appeal rejected imputed ministerial knowledge and upheld orders.

enrichment.short_title: NAHS v Department of Health: lawfulness of kava-kava prohibition orders
key_facts: The Secretary of State prohibited sale of kava-kava for medicinal purposes and banned its use in foodstuffs following hepatotoxicity reports.
Professor Edzard Ernst, a Medicines Commission member, opposed the ban and had published a meta-analysis questioning the safety evidence.
Claimants argued ministers acted in ignorance of Ernst's expert review and that consultation omitted warning-labelling options.
Crane J dismissed the claim; the Court of Appeal reconsidered whether departmental knowledge could be imputed to ministers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against dismissal of judicial review challenging prohibitory orders made under the Medicines Act 1968 and Food Safety Act 1990.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the medicines Order and food Regulation were upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A minister who personally decides must know the salient legally relevant facts, but civil servants' knowledge is not automatically the minister's knowledge under Bushell; on the facts Lord Hunt knew enough, including Ernst's opposition and a summary of his objections, to lawfully make the prohibition Order.
legal_issues: Whether civil servants' knowledge is imputed to a deciding minister
Whether Lord Hunt failed to take relevant account of Professor Ernst's meta-analysis
Whether consultation was flawed by omitting compulsory warning labelling
Whether omission of a goods-in-transit exemption required quashing the food Regulations
linked_authorities: Carltona Ltd v Commissioners of Works [1943] 2 All ER 560
Bushell v Secretary of State for the Environment [1981] AC 75
Minister for Aboriginal Affairs v Peko-Wallsend Ltd (1986) 162 CLR 24

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate reasoning on ministerial knowledge and each surviving ground of challenge.

notes: Article 141 equal pay appeal on cross-department civil service comparators; appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Robertson: cross-department equal pay comparators and the single source test
key_facts: Six male civil servants in DEFRA sought equal pay by comparison with two female Senior Personal Secretaries in DETR.
All were Crown servants but worked under different departmental pay and conditions after delegation of pay negotiations.
The employment tribunal allowed cross-department comparison; the Employment Appeal Tribunal reversed on Article 141.
It was assumed for the preliminary issue that the applicants and comparators performed work of equal value.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on a preliminary point of law from equal pay proceedings under Article 141 EC.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-departmental comparison was not permitted on the agreed facts.
enrichment.ratio: Article 141 requires pay differences to be attributable to a single source responsible for the inequality; common employment by the Crown is not sufficient where individual departments fix pay after delegated bargaining, so DEFRA and DETR were separate sources.
legal_issues: Whether common Crown employment suffices for Article 141 comparability
Application of the Lawrence single source test to civil servants
Whether departmental pay delegation left the Crown as the responsible body
Whether retained or revocable central powers made the Crown the single source
linked_authorities: Lawrence v Regent Office Care Ltd [2003] ICR 1092
Allonby v Accrington & Rossendale Further Education College [2004] IRLR 224

confidence.notes: Preliminary legal issue and Lawrence application are comprehensively addressed on agreed facts.

notes: Boundary dispute out-of-time appeal application refused after 39-month delay.

enrichment.short_title: Brough v Smith: refusal to extend time to appeal boundary judgment
key_facts: Mr Recorder Hirst fixed the boundary between neighbouring properties at Darras Hall in favour of Dr Smith and Dr Hutchinson and granted a permanent injunction and damages for trespass.
The judge found a 1990 boundary agreement or estoppel based on a wire mesh fence replacing an earlier post and rail fence.
Mr and Mrs Brough sought extension of time and permission to appeal nearly three years after judgment.
They wished to adduce fresh evidence from a former neighbour and a surveyor obtained long after trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for extension of time and permission to appeal from a boundary judgment, heard under CPR 3.9.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; no extension of time or permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: A delay of 39 months without adequate explanation, where grounds existed at judgment, offends the public interest in finality; CPR 3.9 factors, including prejudice from absent trial transcripts and a site inspection, weigh against relief.
legal_issues: Whether extension of time to appeal should be granted under CPR 3.9
Whether unpleaded boundary agreement findings could support an appeal
Admissibility of fresh expert and witness evidence on appeal
Weight to be given to a trial judge's site inspection and fact findings

confidence.notes: Procedural disposition and CPR 3.9 analysis are explicit though merits were not fully retried.

notes: Attorney General reference on unduly lenient deferred sentence for cocaine warehousing.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference No 152 of 2004: unduly lenient deferred sentence for cocaine warehousing
key_facts: A 28-year-old offender pleaded guilty to possession of Class A cocaine with intent to supply and supplying cocaine.
Police found about 249 grams of cocaine in an outhouse and a smaller quantity under his bed; he admitted acting as warehouseman for a dealer, paid in cocaine.
The Crown Court recorder deferred sentence to allow the offender to demonstrate he could overcome addiction.
The Attorney General referred the deferral as unduly lenient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference on the ground that deferring sentence was unduly lenient for a Class A drug warehousing offence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; deferred sentence replaced with two years' imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Warehousing is an important role in the drug supply chain and ordinarily requires immediate custody; personal mitigation and payment in drugs may reduce the starting point, but double jeopardy on a reference does not avoid a minimum custodial sentence here.
legal_issues: Whether deferring sentence was unduly lenient for warehousing 253.7 grams of cocaine
The appropriate starting point for a warehouseman after guilty plea
Effect of payment in drugs rather than cash profit
Application of double jeopardy principles on an Attorney General's reference

confidence.notes: Facts, sentencing principles and substituted sentence are clearly stated.

notes: CMR carrier liability for stolen processors; claim succeeded but damages capped at £657.73.

enrichment.short_title: Datec v UPS: CMR liability for loss of computer processor shipment

statutes_considered.title: Carriage of Goods by Road Act 1965
Convention on the Contract for the International Carriage of Goods by Road (CMR)

key_facts: Datec and Incoparts consigned computer processors worth about £241,000 from Milton Keynes to Amsterdam via UPS in July 2002.
The goods did not arrive at the consignee's agent; the claimants alleged theft by UPS employees at the Cologne-Amsterdam stage.
UPS relied on standard terms including a $50,000 value restriction and CMR compensation limits.
The claimants argued wilful misconduct prevented UPS from relying on Article 23 limitation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of a claim for loss of goods in international road carriage under the CMR.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded but damages limited to £657.73 under Article 23 of the CMR.
enrichment.ratio: UPS were liable under Article 17.1 for loss between takeover and delivery, but the claimants failed to show wilful misconduct or equivalent default so Article 23 limitation applied; wrongful declaration of value did not break the causal chain for Article 17.2 defences.
legal_issues: Whether UPS failed to deliver the consignment and were liable under Article 17.1
Whether employee theft amounted to wilful misconduct defeating Article 23
Effect of UPS terms restricting declared shipment value
Whether loss arose from the sender's wrongful acts under Article 17.2

confidence.notes: Liability and limitation conclusions are explicit; detailed fact findings on theft were resolved at trial.

notes: Quantum appeal on defective fish dryer; loss of profit reduced for 2003-2004 and set-off allowed.

enrichment.short_title: Scott Equipment v Russell Grant: quantum of loss of profit for defective fish dryer
key_facts: Russell Grant bought a waste fish drying plant from Scott Equipment that never met the contracted throughput specification.
Holland J found breach after a nine-month commissioning period and awarded about £1 million loss of profit plus other sums.
From April 2003 Grants sharply reduced use of the plant despite it then operating at about 70% of warranted capacity.
Scotts appealed on quantum only, including a £50,000 unpaid instalment and loss periods after March 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on permission granted as to quantum after trial finding liability for breach of a supply contract.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; damages reduced by removing 2003-2004 loss of profit awards and adjusting for set-off of pre-commission fire damage costs against the £50,000 counterclaim.
enrichment.ratio: Where reduced throughput after March 2003 was not caused by the breach, the claimant failed to prove continuing loss of profit; a sum not recoverable as damages because of limitation may still be set off against a separate debt unless expressly waived.
legal_issues: Whether loss of profit after 30 March 2003 was caused by Scott Equipment's breach
Whether Grants failed to mitigate by reducing plant use
Whether the £50,000 final instalment was due under the contract
Whether pre-commission fire damage costs could be set off against the counterclaim

confidence.notes: Quantum grounds and appellate adjustments are detailed, though some trial findings on mitigation were inferential.

notes: Data Protection Act subject access claim against Lloyds; unstructured files held not data or personal data.

enrichment.short_title: Smith v Lloyds TSB: subject access request for unstructured bank files
key_facts: Terence Smith sought disclosure under section 7 of documents held by Lloyds relating to loans to his company Display Electronics Ltd and an alleged oral funding agreement.
Lloyds held no computerised records and kept unstructured paper bundles in boxes without a relevant filing system.
Smith argued once-processed and scannable documents should count as data under the 1998 Act.
Previous litigation had determined against the existence of the alleged oral agreement with the bank.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery Division claim under section 7(9) of the Data Protection Act 1998 for an order requiring subject access.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no order for disclosure under section 7.
enrichment.ratio: Information in unstructured manual files is not data under the 1998 Act unless part of a relevant filing system at the date of the request; the once-processed argument fails because status is assessed at request date, and company loan documents mentioning Smith are not his personal data under Durant.
legal_issues: Whether unstructured manual bank files constitute data under the 1998 Act
Whether previously computer-processed information remains data after manual storage only
Whether scannability creates a relevant filing system
Whether the requested documents were personal data relating to Mr Smith
linked_authorities: Durant v Financial Services Authority [2003] EWCA Civ 1746
Johnson v Medical Defence Union [2004] EWHC 347

confidence.notes: Legal conclusions on data, personal data and discretion follow detailed statutory and Durant analysis.

notes: Debt trial where defendants shut out for no witness statements; appeal allowed on stringent terms.

enrichment.short_title: Primus v Pan European: trial sanctions and adjournment in debt claim
key_facts: Company officers signed a compromise agreement to pay about €1 million in instalments for unpaid pre-paid calling card supplies.
Primus sued in debt; defendants pleaded the agreement was signed in escrow pending verification of call detail records.
At trial the defendants had not filed witness statements and claimed no notice until the day before; their solicitor had written warning of lack of instructions.
The judge refused adjournment, debarring defendants from giving evidence, and entered judgment for the claimants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against judgment entered at trial after refusal to adjourn and application of CPR 32.10 sanctions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment set aside subject to payment of £6,000 costs and £300,000 into court within 21 days, otherwise judgment stands.
enrichment.ratio: When deciding sanctions under CPR 3.9 and 32.10 together, the court must systematically balance prejudice; debarring a pleaded defence to a substantial debt claim was unjust where an adjournment on stringent terms would not materially prejudice the claimant.
legal_issues: Whether the judge should have adjourned rather than proceed to trial
Whether defendants should have been permitted to give oral evidence without witness statements
Proper application of CPR 3.9 when considering relief from sanctions
Whether Article 6 required allowing the defence to be heard
linked_authorities: De Haes and Gijsels v Belgium (1997) 24 EHRR 1

confidence.notes: Procedural reasoning and conditional appellate order are clearly set out.

notes: Search order case; privilege against self-incrimination waived; copy of paedophile material to be sent to prosecutors.

enrichment.short_title: O Ltd v Z: search order, privilege and paedophile material found on seized computers
key_facts: An employer obtained an ex parte search order against a former employee suspected of taking confidential business material.
During the search the employee handed computer material to the court-appointed expert; later examination revealed serious paedophile images unrelated to the claim.
The employee had not been told of the privilege against self-incrimination in the search order or by the supervising solicitor.
The expert sought directions to pass the material to the prosecuting authority.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application for directions on use and disclosure of material seized under a search order in intellectual property proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Privilege held waived; the expert directed to provide a copy of the offensive material to the prosecuting authority while originals remain under court control.
enrichment.ratio: The privilege against self-incrimination was lost when the defendant voluntarily handed the offensive material to the expert without claiming privilege; a civil court cannot override the privilege by balancing exercise, but voluntary disclosure to a third party defeats it objectively.
legal_issues: Whether privilege against self-incrimination applied to material seized under a search order
Whether the defendant waived privilege by handing material to the expert
Whether fruits of an IP search order could be used for criminal prosecution
What directions should govern disclosure to the prosecuting authority
linked_authorities: Rank Film Distributors Ltd v Video Information Centre [1982] AC 380
Lock International plc v Beswick [1989] 1 WLR 1268

confidence.notes: Final directions and waiver reasoning are explicit though broader law reform observations are obiter.
